    "text": "# MEGADOCK\n\n**MEGADOCK** is an ultra-high-performance protein-protein prediction software for heterogeneous supercomputers using FFT-grid-based docking with MPI/OpenMP/GPU parallelization.\n\n[![License: CC BY-NC 4.0](https://licensebuttons.net/l/by-nc/4.0/80x15.png)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/) \n[![License: CC BY-NC 4.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-CC%20BY--NC%204.0-lightgrey.svg)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/)\n\n![Build Status](https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK/workflows/Build%20containers/badge.svg?branch=master)\n\n\n## Target Environments\n\n| Type | Target Env.     | Approach           |\n|:----:|-----------------|--------------------|\n|  (a) | GPU cluster     | GPU + OpenMP + MPI |\n|  (b) | CPU cluster     | OpenMP + MPI       |\n|  (c) | GPU node        | GPU + OpenMP       |\n|  (d) | CPU node        | OpenMP             |\n\n\n## Installation and Command Details\n\nFor installation and command details, please read appropriate section on followings:\n- Read command and script details\n  - [doc/README.md](./doc/README.md)\n- Build a binary from source code\n  - [doc/BUILD.md](./doc/BUILD.md)\n- Build a docker container image\n  - [doc/README_for_docker.md](doc/README_for_docker.md)\n    - [akiyamalab/megadock](https://hub.docker.com/r/akiyamalab/megadock/) (Docker Hub)\n\n\n## Reference\n\nMasahito Ohue, Takehiro Shimoda, Shuji Suzuki, Yuri Matsuzaki, Takashi Ishida, Yutaka Akiyama. **MEGADOCK 4.0: an ultra-high-performance protein-protein docking software for heterogeneous supercomputers**, *Bioinformatics*, 30(22): 3281-3283, 2014. http://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btu532\n\nMasahito Ohue, Yuri Matsuzaki, Nobuyuki Uchikoga, Takashi Ishida, Yutaka Akiyama. **MEGADOCK: An all-to-all protein-protein interaction prediction system using tertiary structure data**, *Protein and Peptide Letters*, 21(8): 766-778, 2014. https://doi.org/10.2174/09298665113209990050\n\n\n## Older Versions\n\n[http://www.bi.cs.titech.ac.jp/megadock/archives/](http://www.bi.cs.titech.ac.jp/megadock/archives/)\n\n\n## License\n\nMEGADOCK is licensed by CC BY-NC 4.0.     "text": "![pinder](https://github.com/pinder-org/pinder/raw/main/assets/pinder.png)\n<div align=\"center\">\n    <h1>PINDER: The Protein INteraction Dataset and Evaluation Resource</h1>\n</div>\n\n---\n\n[![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/pinder)](https://pypi.org/project/pinder/)\n[![license](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-blue.svg)](https://github.com/pinder-org/pinder/blob/master/LICENSE)\n[![GitHub Repo stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/pinder-org/pinder)](https://github.com/pinder-org/pinder/stargazers)\n[![test](https://github.com/pinder-org/pinder/actions/workflows/pr.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/pinder-org/pinder/actions/workflows/pr.yaml)\n[![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/pinder-org/pinder/graph/badge.svg?token=NPQAYW75OD)](https://codecov.io/gh/pinder-org/pinder)\n\n# \ud83d\udcda About\n\n**pinder**, short for **p**rotein **in**teraction **d**ataset and **e**valuation **r**esource, is a dataset and resource for training and evaluation of protein-protein docking algorithms. It is ~500x larger than previous state of the art datasets and is the first dataset to include paired predicted and apo structures to train flexible docking methods.\n\nThe complete dataset contains approximately 1.04 TB of files and is hosted on Cloudflare R2 at https://pinderdata.org.\n\n# \ud83d\udc68\u200d\ud83d\udcbb Getting Started\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n### fastpdb support\n\npinder uses [fastpdb](https://github.com/biotite-dev/fastpdb) to accelerate PDB\nI/O operations. fastpdb is a dependency of pinder-core, and pip will attempt to\ninstall it for you during the installation of pinder. Pre-built wheels of\nfastpdb are available on PyPI for the following platforms:\n1. Linux with `glibc>=2.34` (e.g., Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04, RHEL 9, etc.)\n2. MacOS Sierra (10.12) or newer\n3. Windows\n\nIf your platform doesn't match these conditions, you will not get a wheel and\npip will attempt to build fastpdb from source. In order to build fastpdb from\nsource, you will need the rust toolchain, which you can install by running:\n\n```bash\ncurl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh\n```\n\nbefore installing pinder.\n\n## Install pinder\n\n### Initialize a virtual environment or conda environment\n\nWe recommend installing pinder into a clean virtual environment or conda\nenvironment. This can be done using\n[`mamba`](https://github.com/mamba-org/mamba) or `conda` (you can swap `mamba`\nfor `conda` for the same functionality):\n\n\n```bash\nmamba create --name pinder python=3.11\nmamba activate pinder\n```\n\n\nor via `venv` from the Python standard library:\n\n```bash\n# clone the repo and cd into it, unless you plan to install from PyPI, then\npython3 -m venv venv\nsource venv/bin/activate\n```\n\n## Install optional dependencies\n\n### pytorch-cluster\n\n`pytorch-cluster` is an optional dependency for pinder. If you wish to make use\nof its features, you will need to install it separately.\n\nTo install from a wheel, run\n\n```bash\npip install torch-cluster -f https://data.pyg.org/whl/torch-${TORCH}+${CUDA}.html\n```\n\nwhere `${TORCH}` should be replaced by the version of PyTorch installed and `${CUDA}` should be replaced by either `cpu`, `cu118`, or `cu121`\ndepending on your PyTorch installation.\n\nTo install from source, first make sure you have pytorch installed in the\ncurrent environment (`pip install torch`), then run\n\n```bash\npip install torch-cluster\n```\n\nNote that on Apple Silicon MacOS machines, installation from source is the only option.\n\n### PRODIGY-cryst\n\nPRODIGY-cryst is used in the data ingestion pipeline to predict the probability that an interface is a biological interaction. While it is not needed to use `pinder.core`, it is an optional dependency of `pinder.data` and can be installed as a git-based installation. To install, run\n\n```bash\npip install git+https://github.com/yusuf1759/prodigy-cryst.git\n```\n\n### Install pinder packages from PyPI\n\nTo install with the minimal dependencies needed to use `pinder.core`\n```bash\npip install pinder\n```\n\nInstall optional extras, for instance to use the `pinder.eval` package\n\n```bash\npip install pinder[eval]\n```\n\nOr, install all extras\n\n```bash\npip install pinder[all]\n```\n\n\n# \u2b07\ufe0f Getting the dataset\n\nWe strongly recommend to interact via the provided python API in `pinder-core`, as follows, which will automatically download and load the data into either `$PINDER_BASE_DIR` or `$XDG_DATA_HOME` (usually `~/.local/share/pinder` on Mac and Linux) if no explicit download path is provided (recommended)\n\nNOTE: the default location for the dataset is `~/.local/share/pinder/<release version>`\n\nIf you want to use a different location, you can do so by setting the `PINDER_BASE_DIR` environment variable.\n\nThe base dir refers to a fully qualified path name up until the `<release version>` (not inclusive).\n\nFor instance, you could:\n```bash\nexport PINDER_BASE_DIR=~/my-custom-location-for-pinder/pinder\n```\n\nYou can always check the current location of the dataset like so:\n```python\nfrom pinder.core import get_pinder_location\nget_pinder_location()\n```\n\nThe current release version of pinder is `2024-02`.\n\nYou can find the list of available dataset releases and the associated changes in the [data changelog](https://github.com/pinder-org/pinder/blob/main/changelog_data.md).\n\n## Download archives and sync the complete dataset\n\n```bash\npinder_download\npinder_sync_data\n```\n\n`pinder_download` downloads and extracts the published archives. The archives\ndo not contain every file in the release manifests. Run `pinder_sync_data`\nafter extraction to download the missing structure and mapping files and verify\ntheir checksums. Existing files are skipped without checksum verification and\nare not replaced. The index and metadata are downloaded automatically when\nfirst accessed through `get_index()` and `get_metadata()`.\n\nTo inspect the archive download options:\n\n```\npinder_download --help\n\nusage: Download latest pinder dataset to disk [-h] [--pinder_base_dir PINDER_BASE_DIR] [--pinder_release PINDER_RELEASE] [--skip_inflation]\n\noptional arguments:\n  -h, --help            show this help message and exit\n  --pinder_base_dir PINDER_BASE_DIR\n                        specify a non-default pinder base directory\n  --pinder_release PINDER_RELEASE\n                        specify a pinder dataset version\n  --skip_inflation      if passed, will only download the compressed archives without unpacking\n```\n\nThe full dataset should look like this:\n\n```bash\nget_pinder_location()/\n    pdbs/\n    test_set_pdbs/\n    mappings/\n    index.parquet\n    metadata.parquet\n```\n\n* `pdbs/` contains individual monomer and ground-truth dimer PDB structures\n* `mappings/` contains mapping information for holo and apo monomers for PDB<->uniprot, as well as original PDB assembly information used in some utilities\n* `index.parquet` contains the master index of every dimer in pinder. See [here](https://pinder-org.github.io/pinder/pinder-index.html) for more details.\n* `metadata.parquet` contains additional metadata detail for each entry in the index.\n\nDownloads are served from `https://pinderdata.org/2024-02/`. Use\n`pinder_download` above to download archives with checksum verification and\nresume during automatic retries.\n\nFor the default archive-download-and-sync workflow, allow at least **1.2 TB of\nfree disk space**, including room for filesystem overhead. Sizes below use\ndecimal units (1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes) and describe the `2024-02` release:\n\n| Data | Compressed archive | Complete directory from manifest |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |\n| PDB structures | 168.88 GB | 1,013.35 GB |\n| Test-set structures | 0.18 GB | 0.73 GB |\n| Mappings | 7.23 GB | 23.83 GB |\n\nThe archives total approximately 176.3 GB; the complete directories total\napproximately 1.04 TB. `pinder_download` removes each archive after extraction.\nKeeping archives with `--skip_inflation` and later retaining them alongside the\ncomplete dataset requires additional space.\n\n## Updating the dataset\nIn the event that there are patch (non-breaking) changes to the index or metadata, you can sync your local copy of the index using a similar command-line interface:\n\n```\npinder_update_index --help\n\nusage: Download latest pinder index to disk [-h] [--pinder_base_dir PINDER_BASE_DIR] [--pinder_release PINDER_RELEASE] [--skip_inflation]\n\noptional arguments:\n  -h, --help            show this help message and exit\n  --pinder_base_dir PINDER_BASE_DIR\n                        specify a non-default pinder base directory\n  --pinder_release PINDER_RELEASE\n                        specify a pinder dataset version\n```\n\nTo fetch additional structure or mapping files listed in the release manifests,\nrun `pinder_sync_data`. It downloads missing files; it does not verify or replace\nexisting local files. Dataset changes are announced in the\n[data changelog](https://github.com/pinder-org/pinder/blob/main/changelog_data.md).\nTo inspect the sync options:\n\n```\npinder_sync_data --help\nusage: Sync missing pinder structural data files to disk [-h] [--pinder_base_dir PINDER_BASE_DIR] [--pinder_release PINDER_RELEASE] [--skip_inflation]\n\noptional arguments:\n  -h, --help            show this help message and exit\n  --pinder_base_dir PINDER_BASE_DIR\n                        specify a non-default pinder base directory\n  --pinder_release PINDER_RELEASE\n                        specify a pinder dataset version\n\n```\n\n\n# Pinder datasets & resources\n\n## 1. \ud83c\udfc5 Gold standard benchmark sets\nA set of 4 interface structure & sequence-deleaked, gold standard benchmark sets, all of which were redundancy removed and filtered to be of highest quality\n\n| Dataset         |   # of PDB IDs |   # of Clusters |   # Holo pairs |   # Apo pairs |   # AF2 Pairs | Description |\n|:----------------|---------------:|----------------:|---------------:|--------------:|--------------:|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| PINDER-XL       |           1955 |            1955 |           1955 |           342 |          1747 | Full test set, 1,955 cluster representatives, including 342 apo paired structures and 1,747 AFDB structures PINDER-XL, comprised of 250 clusters (188 heterodimer and 62 homodimers) sampled for diverse Uniprot and PFAM annotations, 93 of which have apo paired structures (143 have at least one apo monomer) and all of which have paired AFDB structures, to evaluate methods for which sampling from the full set is too slow                              |\n| PINDER-AF2      |            180 |             180 |            180 |            30 |           127 | A smaller subset of PINDER-XL, comprised of 180 clusters, 30 of which have paired apo structures and 131 with paired AFDB structures, which were deleaked against the AF2MM training set with a more rigorous deleaking process to remove any members with interfaces similar to the AF2MM training set as determined by iAlign, to evaluate methods against AF2MM                                                                                                                                                |\n\n\nAll of these contain ready to use, pre-rotated & translated monomer structures\n\n\n**A validation holdout set:**\n\n| Dataset   |   # of PDB IDs |   # of Clusters |   # Holo pairs |   # Apo pairs |   # AF2 Pairs | Description |\n|:----------|---------------:|----------------:|---------------:|--------------:|--------------:|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| Val       |           1958 |            1958 |           1958 |           342 |          1789 | Validation set, consisting of 1,958 cluster representatives, of which 342 have paired apo structures and 1,789 of which have paired AFDB structures |\n\n\n**A training set which provides an extensive number of possible training examples:**\n\n|                              | Dataset                      | Train                                                                                                                                                           |\n| Size<sup>1</sup>             | 2456152                                                                                                                                                         |\n| Theoretical Size<sup>2</sup> | 25130994                                                                                                                                                        |\n| # of PDB IDs                 | 62706                                                                                                                                                           |\n| # of Clusters                | 42220                                                                                                                                                           |\n| # Apo Pairs                  | 136498                                                                                                                                                          |\n| # AF2 Pairs                  | 566171                                                                                                                                                          |\n| # At least one Apo Monomer   | 274194                                                                                                                                                          |\n| # At least one AF2 Monomer   | 621276                                                                                                                                                          |\n| Description Size refers to the sum of training examples with at least one Apo monomer (274,194), at least one AF2 monomer (621,276), and the holo monomers (1,560,682)\n2. Theoretical size refers to the theoretical number of training examples made available by pinder. It includes all of the available Apo monomers for each of receptor and ligand, respectively, and all of the combinations with other monomer types. E.g., holo-receptor + apo-ligand1, AF2-receptor + apo-ligand2, etc.\n\n\n\nSee [Dataset Generation](#-dataset-generation) for details on how the dataset was generated.\n\n##  2. \ud83d\udcca Leaderboard\nA **leaderboard** of the current state of the art physics-based docking methods as reference\n\n| Type    | Name       | Train Dataset | Leaderboards\n|---------|------------|---------| ----|\n| Physics | FroDock    | N/A     | `PINDER-XL`, `PINDER-S`, `PINDER-AF2` |\n| Physics | PatchDock  | N/A     |`PINDER-XL`, `PINDER-S`, `PINDER-AF2` |\n| Physics | HDock      | N/A     |`PINDER-XL`, `PINDER-S`, `PINDER-AF2` |\n| ML      | DiffDock-PP| pinder-holo    |`PINDER-XL`, `PINDER-S`, `PINDER-AF2` |\n| ML      | AF2-MM    | af2mm    |`PINDER-AF2` |\n\n\n## 3. \u2696\ufe0f Evaluation harness\n\nA complete evaluation harness with a set of highly efficient pure-python or rust implementations of standard metrics for evaluation, such as DockQ is provided.\n\nWe use the community-standard CAPRI metrics for assessing docking methods. Further detail can be found [here](https://predictioncenter.org/casp15/doc/presentations/Day2/Assessment_Assembly-CAPRI_MLensink.pdf)\n\nThe evaluation harness can be used either through methods in pinder.eval or as a CLI script:\n\n```\npinder_eval --help\n\nusage: pinder_eval [-h] --eval_dir eval_dir [--serial] [--method_name method_name] [--allow_missing] [--custom_index CUSTOM_INDEX] [--max_workers MAX_WORKERS]\n\noptions:\n  -h, --help            show this help message and exit\n  --eval_dir eval_dir, -f eval_dir\n                        Path to eval\n  --serial, -s          Whether to disable parallel eval over systems\n  --method_name method_name, -m method_name, -n method_name\n                        Optional name for output csv\n  --allow_missing, -a   Whether to allow missing systems for a given pinder-set + monomer\n  --custom_index CUSTOM_INDEX, -c CUSTOM_INDEX\n                        Optional local filepath or R2 URL to a custom index with non-pinder splits. Note: must still follow the pinder index schema and define test holdout sets, but does not need to share the same\n                        split members.\n  --max_workers MAX_WORKERS, -w MAX_WORKERS\n                        Optional maximum number of processes to spawn in multiprocessing. Default is None (all available cores).\n```\n\nThe expected format for the contents of `eval_dir` are shown below:\n```\neval_dir_example/\n\u2514\u2500\u2500 some_method\n    \u251c\u2500\u2500 1an1__A1_P00761--1an1__B1_P80424\n    \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u251c\u2500\u2500 apo_decoys\n    \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u251c\u2500\u2500 model_1.pdb\n    \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u2514\u2500\u2500 model_2.pdb\n    \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u251c\u2500\u2500 holo_decoys\n    \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u251c\u2500\u2500 model_1.pdb\n    \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u2514\u2500\u2500 model_2.pdb\n    \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u2514\u2500\u2500 predicted_decoys\n    \u2502\u00a0\u00a0     \u251c\u2500\u2500 model_1.pdb\n    \u2502\u00a0\u00a0     \u2514\u2500\u2500 model_2.pdb\n    \u2514\u2500\u2500 1b8m__A1_P23560--1b8m__B1_P34130\n        \u251c\u2500\u2500 holo_decoys\n        \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u251c\u2500\u2500 model_1.pdb\n        \u2502\u00a0\u00a0 \u2514\u2500\u2500 model_2.pdb\n        \u2514\u2500\u2500 predicted_decoys\n            \u251c\u2500\u2500 model_1.pdb\n            \u2514\u2500\u2500 model_2.pdb\n```\n\nThe eval directory should contain one or more methods to evaluate as sub-directories.\n\nEach method sub-directory should contains sub-directories that are named by pinder system ID.\n\nInside of each pinder system sub-directory, you should have three subdirectories:\n* `holo_decoys` (predictions that were made using holo monomers)\n* `apo_decoys` (predictions made using apo monomers)\n* `predicted_decoys` (predictions made using predicted, e.g. AF2, monomers)\n\nYou can have any number of decoys in each directory; however, the decoys should be named in a way that the prediction rank can be extracted. In the above example, the decoys are named using a `model_<rank>.pdb` convention. Other names for decoy models are accepted, so long as they can match the regex pattern used in `pinder.eval.dockq.MethodMetrics`: `r\"\\d+(?=\\D*$)\"`\n\nEach model decoy should have exactly two chains: {R, L} for {Receptor, Ligand}, respectively.\n\n\n\u26a0\ufe0f **Note: in order to make a fair comparison of methods across complete test sets, if a method is missing predictions for a system, the following metrics are used as a penalty**\n\n```python\n\n{\n    \"iRMS\": 100.0,\n    \"LRMS\": 100.0,\n    \"Fnat\": 0.0,\n    \"DockQ\": 0.0,\n    \"CAPRI\": \"Incorrect\",\n}\n```\n\nFor more details on the implementations of the eval metrics, see the [eval tutorial](https://pinder-org.github.io/pinder/pinder-eval.html), [API docs](https://pinder-org.github.io/pinder/source/pinder.eval.dockq.html#) and [eval FAQ](https://pinder-org.github.io/pinder/faq.html#how-can-i-use-the-evaluation-harness-outside-of-a-pinder-context).\n\nFor more details on leaderboard generation, see the [MethodMetrics](https://github.com/pinder-org/pinder/blob/main/src/pinder-eval/pinder/eval/dockq/method.py) implementation.\n\n\n## 4. \ud83e\uddea Training set\n\nWe provide a ready-to-use, large training set, `PINDER-Train` with **2,456,152** pairs, consisting of 1,560,682 bound structures, 274,194 structures with at least one paired apo structure and 621,276 pairs with at least one paired AFDB structures. These can be combined to yield up to 25,130,994 unique training examples.\nThey are clustered by __interface__ similarity via FoldSeek and deleaked by structure and interface similarity against the `PINDER-XL` (and thus against all others) and validation set, `PINDER-Val`.\n\n`PINDER-Val` is included as a redundancy removed validation set of 1,958 holo structures from 1,958 clusters, prepared in identical fashion and distribution to the test set, including 342 apo paired structures and 1,789 AFDB structures, filtered with the same quality criteria as the test set to allow for representative monitoring of training performance.\n\nSee [Dataset Generation](#-dataset-generation) for details on how the dataset was generated.\n\n## 5. \ud83d\udce6 Dataloader\n\nWe provide two flavors of dataloaders based on the `Dataset` and `DataLoader` APIs from `torch` and `torch-geometric` as example implementations (and are happy to provide more if there are feature requests) for easy loading of datasets.\n\nAll dataloaders are based on iterators over `PinderSystem`, a core abstraction which provides the collection of structural data associated with an entry in the pinder database.\n\nThe `PinderSystem` exposes the following structures:\n* Ground-truth crystal structure\n* Holo receptor and ligand\n* Apo receptor and ligand (where available)\n* Predicted receptor and ligand (currently from alphafold; where available)\n\n**Note: all monomers follow the chain naming convention of R, L for receptor and ligand, respectively. However, if you are using the PDB files directly without `PinderSystem`, note that the apo and predicted monomers are both stored with chain ID A. This was done to reduce file/disk burden by not duplicating apo/predicted monomers that map to both receptor and/or ligand across multiple systems.**\n\n\nEach structure is defined by the `Structure` abstraction. None,\n    pre_transform: Callable[[PinderSystem], PinderSystem] | None = None,\n    pre_filter: Callable[[PinderSystem], PinderSystem | bool] | None = None,\n    limit_by: int | None = None,\n int = 10,\n)\n\nloader = get_geo_loader(train_dataset)\n```\n\n**Note: this is only one example of a featurizer that illustrates how to construct a hetero graph from a `PinderSystem` object.**\n\nWe Most evidently, `pinder` is currently focusing on biological dimers. As more methods expand beyond dimers, such as via co-folding approaches, `pinder` will be generalized to higher-order oligomers. Additionally, there are a few smaller methodological limitations - for instance, the reliance on single reference conformations and the inherent bias towards homodimers in the dataset can impact the accuracy and generalizability of the models.\n\nFurther, improvements in *apo* pairing and the integration of more advanced tools, such as `iAlign`, into the alignment methodology could enhance the dataset's precision. Addressing these limitations could lead to even larger datasets, better performance and evaluation in future iterations of `pinder`. We provide a more detailed discussion of the limitations of the `pinder` dataset and methodology in [limitations](limitations.md). Below we summarize some key areas of future work:\n\n- [ ] Expansion to higher-order oligomers\n- [ ] Homologous *apo* pairing via Foldseek and MMseqs2 monomer matching\n- [ ] Rosetta-relaxed unbound structures & evaluation set for all structures in the dataset\n- [ ] A complete evaluation harness for reference-free metrics to evaluate the quality of the predicted structures, such as VoroMQA, PISA, and more\n- [ ] Confirmed negative pairs\n- [ ] Addition of an antibody-focused benchmark test set `pinder-ab`\n- [ ] Contact-conditioned benchmarks\n- [ ] Additional information for multimeric training examples (e.g. restraints)\n- [ ] Improved abstractions for pytorch-lightning data loaders\n\n\n# \ud83d\udc68\u200d\ud83d\udcbb Code organization\n\nThis code is split into 4 subpackages\n\n- `pinder-core`: core data structures for interacting with and loading the dataset. includes a pytorch dataloader\n- `pinder-data`: core code for generating the dataset, starting with downloading from the RCSB NextGen rsync server.\n- `pinder-eval`: evaluation harness for the dataset that takes as an input predicted and ground truth structures in a pre-determined folder structure and returns a leaderboard-ready set of entries\n- `pinder-methods`: implementations of the methods in the leaderboard that leverage pinder-primitives for training & running\n\n# \ud83d\udcbd Dataset Generation\n\nThe above datasets was generated using the following steps:\n\n## \ud83d\udeaa Input\n\nThe RCSB NextGen database (as of 01.29.2024) was used as the starting point. All mmCIF files were obtained and representative biological assemblies were generated.\n\n- **PDB PPIs**: Protein-Protein Interactions (PPIs) were detected as all pairs of chains with a backbone atom in contact at a 10\u00c5 threshold.\n- **PDB Monomers for apo structures**: All monomeric PDB entries with the same UniProt ID as a monomer in the dimer PPI entries were aligned (using the UniProt numbering) to the corresponding PPI entry. A suite of evaluation metrics was calculated and only validated pairings were kept. For each dimer monomer, a single apo monomer was chosen as the canonical pair based on a normalized score derived from the evaluation metrics. The rest are made available as alternate apo pairings.\n- **AFDB Monomers for af2 structures**: AFDB entries with the same UniProt ID as PPI entries were aligned (using UniProt numbering) to the corresponding PPI entry.\n\n## \u2139\ufe0f Annotation\n\nAnnotations were obtained from the RCSB NextGen database. The following annotations are included:\n\n1. Oligomeric state of the protein complex (homodimer, heterodimer, oligomer or higher-order\ncomplexes)\n2. Structure determination method (X-Ray, CryoEM, NMR)\n3. Resolution\n4. Interfacial gaps, defined as structurally-unresolved segments on PPI interfaces\n5. Number of distinct atom types. Many earlier Cryo-EM structures contain only a few atom-types\nsuch as only C\u03b1 or backbone atoms\n6. Whether the interface is likely to be a physiological or crystal contact, annotated using Prodigy\n7. Structural elongation, defined as the maximum variance of coordinates projected onto the largest\nprincipal component. This allows detection of long end-to-end stacked complexes, likely to be\nrepetitive with small interfaces\n8. Planarity, defined as deviation of interfacial C\u03b1 atoms from the fitted plane. This interface\ncharacteristic quantifies interfacial shape complementarity. Transient complexes have smaller\nand more planar interfaces than permanent and structural scaffold complexes\n9. Number of components, defined as the number of connected components of a 10\u00c5 C\u03b1 radius\ngraph. This allows detection of structurally discontinuous domains\n10. Intermolecular contacts (labeled as polar or apolar)\n\n## \ud83d\udc65 Clustering\n\nThe clustering works as follows\n- We first define all possible interacting pairs as holo systems by taking chain pair with any residues within a 10\u00c5 backbone atom distance threshold between the interacting chains\n- All-vs-all structural alignments of complete chains were performed using FoldSeek. Note that foldseek uses both sequence (blosum matrix) and structure (3di matrix) to define similar pairs\n- We start by construct a graph with chains as nodes\n- An edge is then added between any two nodes with over 50% foldseek-alignment coverage of the interface residues (as defined above)\n- This will connect any two chains where a substantial part of the interface is similar in either sequence or structure\n- Community clustering via asynchronous label propagation was then performed on this graph to obtain interface clusters. Clusters are used in three ways:\n    - Non-redundant sampling and weighing scheme during training\n    - Non-redundant test/val selection by selecting test as cluster representatives\n    - Deleaking by removal of other cluster members after a member of the cluster is chosen as test/val (Note: deleaking algorithm uses further steps to ensure no-leakage between test/val and train)\n- From the chain-graph clusters we create paired-interface clusters paired-interface cluster of each PPI as $\\{c_{a}, c_{b}\\}$, where $c_a$ and $c_b$ are the interface cluster identifiers for the two interacting chains.\n\n## \ud83e\udded Test filters\n\nSampling for the test and validation sets was performed based on the following criteria:\n\n- Physiological contact (from PRODIGY-cryst)\n- Dimers (to guarantee full bioassembly available during inference)\n- `X-RAY DIFFRACTION` experimental method\n- Resolution $\\leq$ 3.5\u00c5\n- Minimum individual chain length $\\geq$ 40 residues\n- Elements $\\geq$ 3\n- Interface atom gaps at 4\u00c5 threshold = 0\n- Maximum variance $\\leq$ 0.98\n- Single component\n\nAll clusters where any one member passed the above criteria were kept. These filters resulted in 32,775 PPIs (we call these proto-test) in 5,047 clusters (used for val/**PINDER-XL**).\n\nPPIs which passed the criteria in these sampled clusters were deleaked by an additional transitive neighbor search, where any system that had a transitive hit within a depth of 2 in the foldseek graph, but a different cluster ID, was removed. Leaky systems were kept, but assigned a split label of `invalid`. Eligible systems were ranked by heterodimer vs. homodimer (heterodimer preferred), whether they pass the `PINDER-AF2` criteria, and availability of apo and AFDB paired structures. 1 PPI was sampled from each cluster based on the member ranked by the criteria.\n\n\n## \ud83d\udd2a Split\n\nThe dataset was split as follows:\n\n- **PINDER-XL**: Sampling from 1,955 clusters resulted in 1,955 members.\n- **PINDER-Val**: Sampling from 1,958 clusters resulted in 1,958 members.\n- **PINDER-Train**: The rest of the clusters (42,220) resulted in 1,560,682 members\n\nFrom the PDB monomer alignments, we obtained a total of 44,330 unique apo structures, corresponding to 41,630 receptor and 36,910 ligand monomers.\nThis corresponds to 274,194 pinder dimers in train, 441 in val and 436 in **PINDER-XL** with at least one matched apo structure.\n\nFrom the AFDB monomer alignments, we obtained a total of 42,827 unique AFDB structures, corresponding to 37,095 receptor and 38,801 ligand monomers.\nThis corresponds to 621,276 pinder dimers in train, 1,817 in val and 1,775 in **PINDER-XL** with at least one matched AFDB monomer structure.\n\nThese were assigned to the respective chain pairs to yield the numbers from above tables.\n\n**PINDER-S** is a subset of **PINDER-XL**, consisting of 250 clusters (188 heterodimer and 62 homodimers) sampled for diverse Uniprot and PFAM annotations, 93 of which have apo paired structures (143 have at least one apo monomer) and all of which have paired AFDB structures, to evaluate methods for which sampling from the full set is too slow.\n\n## \ud83d\uddde\ufe0f AF2mm\n\nClusters which contain only members released after 10.01.2021 (the AlphaFold-2MM cutoff date) were separated into 675 clusters. From these 675 members, we further de-leaked against any similar interfaces found to any other entry released before the cutoff date as determined by `iAlign`. The members which have low or no similarity to AlphaFold2-Multimer training set (180) were assgined to the `PINDER-AF2` set. Those members in the `PINDER-AF2` set are guaranteed to be structurally distinct from AF2-MM 2.3 training data, while the remaining members are only guaranteed to come from entries released after the cutoff date (time-split).\n\n\n# \ud83d\udcf0 Updates & Versioning\n\nDataset and code are versioned independently.\n\nThe dataset is expected to be updated with at at maximum monthly release cycles frequency via `year-month` as subfolders in `pinder`. The current version is `2024-02`\n\nThere are 2 \"types\" of updates:\n\n- minor changes in the index, or addition or change in structures that can be assigned to train without reclustering and adding leakage and thus not invalidating the test set and **not requiring re-evaluation of the leaderboard methods**\n- major addition of structures that require re-clustering and re-assigning of structures to train, validation and test thus **invalidating the leaderboard**\n\nMajor changes may happen with at maximum annual frequency, and will be clearly announced. Methods can choose *not* to update and continue using previous versions of the dataset\n\nThe code is versioned using [semantic versioning](https://semver.org/) and updated regularly and contains integration test to avoid invalidating any results\n\n# Examples & documentation\n\nPackage documentation, including API documentation, [example notebooks](examples/), and supplementary guides, are made available.\n\nTo view the latest documentation, you can checkout the [gh-pages](https://github.com/pinder-org/pinder/tree/gh-pages) branch and open the [index.html](https://github.com/pinder-org/pinder/blob/gh-pages/index.html) file in your browser.\n\nAlternatively, you can build the package documentation locally after installing optional documentation dependencies:\n\n```\npip install '.[docs]'\ncd docs/\n./build.sh --open\n```\n\nFor a list of frequently asked questions, check the [FAQ section](faq.md).\n\n# Dev guide\n\n## Dev mode install\n\n### Clone the repo\n\nFor http:\n```bash\ngit clone https://github.com/pinder-org/pinder.git\n```\n\nOr ssh:\n```bash\ngit clone git@github.com:pinder-org/pinder.git\n```\n\n### Initialize a conda env\n\n```bash\ncd pinder\nmamba create --name pinder python=3.11\nmamba activate pinder\n```\n\n### Install the desired pinder subpackages in dev mode\n\n```bash\npip install -e '.[dev]'\n```\n\n### (Optional) install pre-commit hooks\n\nThese will ensure that code passes the linter before being committed.\n\n    pre-commit install\n\n## Test suite\n\n    tox\n\nWe lint with ruff. See `tox.ini` and `.pre-commit-config.yaml` for details.\n\n## Debugging\n\nIn order to change log levels, set the `LOG_LEVEL` environment variable. For example:\n\n    export LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG\n\n# Contributing\n\nThis is a community effort and as such we highly encourage contributions.\n"

    "text": "# Installation Guide\n\n\n## Target Environments\n\n| Type | Target Env.     | Approach           |\n|:----:|-----------------|--------------------|\n|  (a) | GPU cluster     | GPU + OpenMP + MPI |\n|  (b) | CPU cluster     | OpenMP + MPI       |\n|  (c) | GPU node        | GPU + OpenMP       |\n|  (d) | CPU node        | OpenMP             |\n\n\n## Requirement\n\n| Library                                                         | GPU cluster | CPU cluster | GPU node | CPU node | Note |\n|:----------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------:|:-----------:|:---:|:---:|:------|\n| [FFTW3](http://www.fftw.org)                                    | yes           | yes           | yes   | yes   | `--enable-float` required ([FAQ](http://www.bi.cs.titech.ac.jp/megadock/faq.html))|\n| MPI (e.g. [OpenMPI](http://www.open-mpi.org))                   | yes           | yes           |     |     |       |\n| [CUDA Toolkit](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-zone)          | yes           |             | yes   |     | `ver >= 5.0` required |\n| [CUDA SDK code samples](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-zone) | yes           |             | yes   |     | same version as toolkit |\n\nFor more detailed build information, please reffer to the [FAQ](http://www.bi.cs.titech.ac.jp/megadock/faq.html) page.\n\n\n## Section Link\n\nPlease select appropriate section for your environment:\n\n- [(a) Compile for GPU cluster (GPU & MPI)](#a-compile-for-gpu-cluster-gpu--mpi)\n- [(b) Compile for MPI cluster (MPI)](#b-compile-for-mpi-cluster-mpi)\n- [(c) Compile for GPU node (GPU)](#c-compile-for-gpu-node-gpu)\n- [(d) Compile for CPU node (only thread parallelization)](#d-compile-for-cpu-node-only-thread-parallelization)\n- [Note for compilation](#note-for-compilation)\n----\n\n# (a) Compile for GPU cluster (GPU & MPI)\n\n## 1. Get source code and change directory\n\n```sh\n# from GitHub (clone)\ngit clone https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK.git\ncd MEGADOCK\n\n# from GitHub (zip)\nwget https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK/archive/master.zip\nunzip master.zip\ncd MEGADOCK-master\n```\n\n## 2. Edit Makefile (PATH, options)\n\n```Makefile\nCUDA_INSTALL_PATH ?= your/cuda/toolkit/install/path # default: /usr/local/cuda\nCUDA_SAMPLES_PATH ?= your/cuda/sdk/install/path     # default: /usr/local/cuda/samples\nFFTW_INSTALL_PATH ?= your/fftw/library/install/path # default: /usr/local\nCPPCOMPILER       ?= g++                            # default: g++ (or icpc, others)\nMPICOMPILER       ?= mpicxx                         # default: mpicxx (or others)\nOPTIMIZATION      ?= -O3                            # \nOMPFLAG           ?= -fopenmp                       # default: -fopenmp (g++), or -openmp, -qopenmp (intel)\n```\n\n```Makefile\nUSE_GPU := 1\nUSE_MPI := 1\n```\n\n## 3. generate binary\n\nAfter completion of `make` command, a binary file `megadock-gpu-dp` will be generated.\n\n```sh\n# build a binary\nmake\n\n# see help\nmegadock-gpu-dp -h\n```\n\n----\n\n# (b) Compile for MPI cluster (MPI)\n\n\n## 1. Get source code and change directory\n\n```sh\n# from GitHub (clone)\ngit clone https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK.git\ncd MEGADOCK\n\n# from GitHub (zip)\nwget https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK/archive/master.zip\nunzip master.zip\ncd MEGADOCK-master\n```\n\n## 2. Edit Makefile (PATH, options)\n\n```Makefile\nFFTW_INSTALL_PATH ?= your/fftw/library/install/path # default: /usr/local\nCPPCOMPILER       ?= g++                            # default: g++ (or icpc, others)\nMPICOMPILER       ?= mpicxx                         # default: mpicxx (or others)\nOPTIMIZATION      ?= -O3                            # \nOMPFLAG           ?= -fopenmp                       # default: -fopenmp (g++), or -openmp, -qopenmp (intel)\n```\n\n```Makefile\nUSE_GPU := 0\nUSE_MPI := 1\n```\n\n## 3. generate binary\n\nAfter completion of `make` command, a binary file `megadock-dp` will be generated.\n\n```sh\n# build a binary\nmake\n\n# see help\nmegadock-dp -h\n```\n\n----\n\n# (c) Compile for GPU node (GPU)\n\n## 1. Get source code and change directory\n```sh\n# from GitHub (clone)\ngit clone https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK.git\ncd MEGADOCK\n\n# from GitHub (zip)\nwget https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK/archive/master.zip\nunzip master.zip\ncd MEGADOCK-master\n```\n\n## 2. Edit Makefile (PATH, options)\n\n```Makefile\nCUDA_INSTALL_PATH ?= your/cuda/toolkit/install/path # default: /usr/local/cuda\nCUDA_SAMPLES_PATH ?= your/cuda/sdk/install/path     # default: /usr/local/cuda/samples\nFFTW_INSTALL_PATH ?= your/fftw/library/install/path # default: /usr/local\nCPPCOMPILER       ?= g++                            # default: g++ (or icpc, others)\nOPTIMIZATION      ?= -O3                            # \nOMPFLAG           ?= -fopenmp                       # default: -fopenmp (g++), or -openmp, -qopenmp (intel)\n```\n\n```Makefile\nUSE_GPU := 1\nUSE_MPI := 0\n```\n\n## 3. generate binary\n\nAfter completion of `make` command, a binary file `megadock-gpu` will be generated.\n\n```sh\n# build a binary\nmake\n\n# see help\nmegadock-gpu -h\n```\n\n--------------------------------------------------------\n\n# (d) Compile for CPU node (only thread parallelization)\n\n## 1. Get source code and change directory\n```sh\n# from GitHub (clone)\ngit clone https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK.git\ncd MEGADOCK\n\n# from GitHub (zip)\nwget https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK/archive/master.zip\nunzip master.zip\ncd MEGADOCK-master\n```\n\n## 2. Edit Makefile (PATH, options)\n\n```Makefile\nFFTW_INSTALL_PATH ?= your/fftw/library/install/path # default: /usr/local\nCPPCOMPILER       ?= g++                            # default: g++ (or icpc, others)\nOPTIMIZATION      ?= -O3                            # \nOMPFLAG           ?= -fopenmp                       # default: -fopenmp (g++), or -openmp, -qopenmp (intel)\n```\n\n```\nUSE_GPU := 0\nUSE_MPI := 0\n```\n\n## 3. generate binary\n\nAfter completion of `make` command, a binary file `megadock` will be generated.\n\n```sh\n# build a binary\nmake\n\n# see help\nmegadock -h\n```\n\n----\n\n## Clean up\n\n```sh\n# remove generated files\nmake allclean\n```\n\n----\n\n# Note for compilation\n\n- `USE_MPI` and `USE_GPU` flags in Makefile should be `1` or `0` for all compilations. If the white spaces exist at end of the line, those flags will be ignored.\n- For GPU use, `SM_VERSIONS` can specity the target NVIDIA GPU architectures of the generated binary. Please change it for your target system. (Default: `sm_60`)\n"

    "url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK/9575280c875732553266e26adc607dd892b02616/doc/README.md",
    "text": "# Command Guide\n\nThis documentation show the command usage and examples for protein-protein docking calculation using MEGADOCK.\nIf you do not have any MEGADOCK binary, please read the build documentation ([doc/BUILD.md](./BUILD.md)).\n\n> Note: The sample input files (`.pdb`, `.table`) are stored in `data` directory.\n\n\n## Section Link\n\nPlease select your target environment and check the command example.\n\n| Type | Target Env.     | Binary             | Note \n|:----:|-----------------|--------------------| :-\n|  (a) | [GPU cluster](#command-for-multiple-nodes-environment) | `megadock-gpu-dp`  | multiple nodes\n|  (b) | [CPU cluster](#command-for-multiple-nodes-environment) | `megadock-dp`      | multiple nodes\n|  (c) | [GPU node](#command-for-single-node-environment)      | `megadock-gpu`     | single node\n|  (d) | [CPU node](#command-for-single-node-environment)      | `megadock`         | single node\n\nOther Commands:\n\n| Command    | Note\n| :-         | :-\n| `decoygen` | [Generate decoy pdb files from docking output](#Generate-decoy-from-docking-output)\n| `block`    | [Blocking target residues](#Blocking-target-residues)\n| `ppiscore` | [Protein-Protein interaction prediction](#Protein-Protein-interaction-prediction)\n\n----\n\n# Command for Single Node Environment\n\nTarget Environments:\n  - (c) Compile for GPU node (GPU)\n  - (d) Compile for CPU node (only thread parallelization)\n\n## Command example\n\n```sh\n# (c) GPU single node\n./megadock-gpu -R receptor.pdb -L ligand.pdb -o receptor-ligand.out\n\n# (d) CPU single node\n./megadock -R receptor.pdb -L ligand.pdb -o receptor-ligand.out\n```\n\n### Run small sample\n\n```sh\n# (c) GPU single node\n./megadock-gpu -R data/1gcq_r.pdb -L data/1gcq_l.pdb -o data/1gcq_r-1gcq_l.out\n\n# (d) CPU single node\n./megadock -R data/1gcq_r.pdb -L data/1gcq_l.pdb -o data/1gcq_r-1gcq_l.out\n```\n\n## Parameters for docking calculation\n\n| Required            | Note\n| :-------------------| :-\n| `-R [filename]`     | receptor pdb file (input)\n| `-L [filename]`     | ligand pdb file (input)\n\n\n| Optional                  | default       | Note\n| :------------------------ | :------------ | :-- \n| `-o [filename]`           | $R-$L.out     | output filename (output)\n| `-O`                      |               | output docking detail files\n| `-N [integer]`            | 2000          | set the number of output predictions\n| `-t [integer]`            | 1             | set the number of predictions per each rotation\n| `-F [integer]`            |               | set the number of FFT point (default: none)\n| `-v [float]`              | 1.2 (angstrom)| set the voxel pitch size\n| `-D`                      |               | set the 6 deg. (54000 angles) of rotational sampling (default to none, 15 deg. (3600 angles) of rotational sampling)\n| `-r [integer]`            | 3600          | set the number of rotational sampling angles (54000: 54000 angles, 1: 1 angles, 24: 24 angles, default to 3600 angles)\n| `-e [float]`              | 1.0           | set the electrostatics term ratio\n| `-d [float]`              | 1.0           | set the hydrophobic term ratio\n| `-a [float]`              | -45.0         | set the rPSC receptor core penalty\n| `-b [float]`              | 1.0           | set the rPSC ligand core penalty\n| `-f [1/2/3]`              | 3             | set function (1: rPSC only, 2: rPSC+Elec, 3: rPSC+Elec+RDE, default to 3)\n| `-h`                      |               | show command help\n\n\n----\n\n# Command for Multiple Nodes Environment\n\nTarget Environments:\n- (a) Compile for GPU cluster (GPU & MPI)\n- (b) Compile for CPU cluster (MPI)\n\n## Command example\n\n```sh\n# (a) GPU & MPI (e.g. 4 MPI processes)\nmpirun -n 4 ./megadock-gpu-dp -tb data/SAMPLE.table\n\n# (b) CPU & MPI (e.g. 4 MPI processes)\nmpirun -n 4 ./megadock-dp -tb data/SAMPLE.table\n```\n\n\n## Parameters for parallel execution\n\n| Required                     | Note\n| :----------------------------| :-\n| `-tb [filename] `            | docking table (.table)\n\n\n| Optional                  | default       | Note\n| :------------------------ | :------------ | :-- \n| `-lg [filename]`          | master.log    | log filename\n| `-rt [integer]`           | 0             | the number of retries\n\n\n## Example of docking table (.table)\n\nParameters and docking target list should be written in a text file.\nA table file should have `TITLE` and `PARAM` lines followed by parameters listed by the same order as in the `PARAM` line.\n`SAMPLE.table` file in this package shows an example.\n\n- [data/SAMPLE.table](data/SAMPLE.table)\n\n```\nTITLE=sample jobs\nPARAM=-R $1 -L $2 -O\ndata/1gcq_r.pdb\tdata/1gcq_r.pdb\ndata/1gcq_r.pdb\tdata/1gcq_l.pdb\ndata/1gcq_l.pdb\tdata/1gcq_r.pdb\ndata/1gcq_l.pdb\tdata/1gcq_l.pdb\n```\n\nYou can specify docking parameters loaded by MEGADOCK by setting `PARAM` in the table file.\nLines follows the `PARAM` lines specifies parameters for each docking job which will be distributed to available nodes by MPI.\n\n### More details about parameters for each docking calculation\n\n- [See above section](#Parametersfor-docking-calculation)\n\n----\n\n# Thread parallelization (OpenMP)\n\nMEGADOCK parallelizes rotation calculations by using OpenMP.\nYou can specify the number of OpenMP threads for parallel calculations by environmental variable such as `$OMP_NUM_THREADS`.\n\n```sh\n# e.g.) megadock binary using 8 OpenMP threads\nexport OMP_NUM_THREADS=8\n./megadock -R data/receptor.pdb -L data/ligand.pdb -o data/receptor_ligand.out\n\n# e.g.) each MPI process uses 8 OpenMP threads\nmpirun -n 4 -x OMP_NUM_THREADS=8  ./megadock-dp -tb data/SAMPLE.table\n```\n\n----\n\n\n# Generate decoy from docking output\n\nEach docking job generates docking output file in which rotation angles (x, y, z) of ligand from the initial structure, numbers of voxel translation (x, y, z) from receptor center coordinate and docking scores are listed.  \n\nIf you want to generate decoy pdbfiles, please use `decoygen` command. It is generated together with MEGADOCK binary.\n\n## Command Usage\n\n```sh\n./decoygen [decoy_filename] [used_ligand.pdb] [.outfile] [decoy no.]\n```\n\n\n## Command Example\n\nFor example, the megadock output file was generated as `dock.out` using `rec.pdb` as receputer input and `lig.pdb` as ligand output, and you want to **generate 1st ranked decoy**.\n\n```sh\n# megadock docking calculation\nmegadock -R rec.pdb -L lig.pdb -o dock.out\n\n# generate 1st ranked decoy\n./decoygen lig.1.pdb lig.pdb dock.out 1\ncat rec.pdb lig.1.pdb > decoy.1.pdb\n\n# lig.1.pdb   : rotated and translated lig.pdb\n# decoy.1.pdb : complex pdb file\n```\n\nIf you want to generate all decoys;\n\n```sh\n# megadock docking calculation\nmegadock -R rec.pdb -L lig.pdb -o dock.out\n\n# generate all decoys\nfor i in `seq 1 2000`; do ./decoygen lig.${i}.pdb lig.pdb dock.out $i; cat rec.pdb lig.${i}.pdb > decoy.${i}.pdb; done\n```\n\n----\n\n# Blocking target residues\n\n`block` tool (python script) is to block some residues of a receptor protein from docking.\nIf you know that some residues are not in the binding sides, please list their residue numbers and input `block` tool.\nThis program changes the name of residues to \"BLK\" and prints the new pdb on the screen.\n\n```sh\n./block [pdbfile] [chain] [target residue list]\n# ex)\n# ./block 1gcq_r.pdb B 182-186,189,195-198,204 > blocked.pdb\n```\n\nTarget residues list is separated by commas and no spaces.\nYou can also use `-` (hyphen): \"182-186\" means blocking residues of 182, 183, ..., 186.\nBlocked residues are substituted for 'BLK'.\nUpdated PDB coordinates are written to \"standard output\". MEGADOCK can only block receptor residues.\n\n----\n\n# Protein-Protein interaction prediction\n\nYou can calculates the evaluated value of Protein-Protein Interaction scores (PPI score) by using `ppiscore` command which is written in perl script.\n\n## Command Example\n\n```sh\n# 1. Docking calculation using MEGADOCK with `-t=3` option\nmegadock -R rec.pdb -L lig.pdb -o dock.out -t 3 -N 10800\n\n# -t: the number of predictions per each rotation\n# -N: the number of output predictions\n\n\n# 2. Output PPI score\n./ppiscore dock.out 10800\n```\n\n### Note\n\n`ppiscore` is compatible with re-ranking tools to get better docking candidates (e.g. [ZRANK1](http://zdock.umassmed.edu/software/)) and those tools can be used for the output files of docking calculation using megadock.\nIf you want to use such reranking tools, please refer to [our website documentation](http://www.bi.cs.titech.ac.jp/megadock/ppi.html).\n\nFor more details about `ppiscore`, please check [our webpage documentation](http://www.bi.cs.titech.ac.jp/megadock/ppi.html) or following references.\n\n----\n\n\n## References\n\n- Masahito Ohue, Takehiro Shimoda, Shuji Suzuki, Yuri Matsuzaki, Takashi Ishida, Yutaka Akiyama. ## Comparison request (science step s29)

This request asks for one comparison-mode run: the arms, fixture inputs, outputs and evaluator exactly as the comparison view (`comparison_view.json`) describes them. It is a recording run on fixture inputs, repeating an earlier recording run of this route with corrections to how the programs are built, how the evaluator is invoked, and how the harness scripts get their data on the box. It is not the seed's main experiment, and the seed's four cases above are not run, fetched or evaluated in it. Preserve the seed above.

What the run does

- Four arms, as the view describes them. A0 is the published baseline (the seed's configuration 1). A1 is the seed's configuration 2. A2 repeats A0's commands and A3 repeats A1's commands, each as separate invocations. The pipeline runs every arm's commands itself; the adapters only check that the input's prepared files exist.
- Four fixture inputs, as the view describes them: holo test-set monomer pairs of four PINDER `2024-02` systems that are not among the seed's four cases. Each input's `spec` names its receptor and ligand sources (URL, byte count, SHA-256), the prepared paths the arms read, and its native complex, which only the evaluator may read.
- The evaluator: PINDER's DockQ implementation at the pinned commit, as the view describes it, scoring each arm's assembled models of one input against that input's native complex.
- Outputs, as the view describes them: the ranked rows of each arm's `docking.out` (transform fields and score field), the coordinates of the assembled models, and the evaluator's DockQ value for each model. They are recorded and compared across arms by the pipeline. No agent computes or reports a comparison.

Which harness files reach the box (correction)

- The pipeline uploads only these files from `harness/` to the box: `setup.sh`, `run_anchors.sh`, `run_command.sh`; `run_evaluation.sh`, `run_units.sh` and `units.json` when they exist; and the sealed comparison files `arms/<arm id>.sh`, `cmp_files.json`, `cmp_extract.json`, `versions.sh`, `fetch_private.sh` and `evaluate.sh`. Any other file written under `harness/` (a Python helper, a JSON list of inputs, a table of published values) never reaches the box. A repair may change only `setup.sh` (or `run_anchors.sh` and `run_command.sh`); the sealed comparison files are never repaired, so a defect in one of them stops the run.
- Every one of these scripts is therefore self-contained: it reads no file under `harness/` except itself, and carries in its own text every list, value and program it needs, or reads it from the variables the pipeline sets (`CMP_INPUT`, `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`, `CMP_OUT`, `CMP_ARM_OUT`, `CMP_EVAL_OUT`, `CMP_PRIVATE`). Write no other file under `harness/`.
- `fetch_private.sh` runs as a separate user with the private directory as its working directory and has no `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`; its output is not kept. It carries in its own text, for each of the four inputs, the native complex's name, URL, byte count and SHA-256 exactly as `spec.reference` gives them in the view, downloads each one, checks its byte count and SHA-256 (a mismatch exits nonzero), and writes it under its working directory at that name.
- `evaluate.sh` takes the input id from `CMP_INPUT` and the native complex's name, byte count and SHA-256 from `spec.reference` in `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`; it reads no input list from any file.

Materials, pins and preparation

- MEGADOCK: the published repository https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK at commit `9575280c875732553266e26adc607dd892b02616`, built twice from the same checkout under `baseline-published/megadock/` in the shared run directory, so that `baseline-published/megadock/megadock`, `baseline-published/megadock/megadock-gpu` and `baseline-published/megadock/decoygen` exist there. The CUDA samples headers come from https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples at tag `v12.8`; they are build dependencies only. The CPU build uses single-precision FFTW exactly as below. The GPU build keeps `-Xcompiler -fopenmp` and `-use_fast_math` and the libraries below, and targets the compute capability of the GPU on this box: `setup.sh` reads it with `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_cap --format=csv,noheader` (for example `8.6` gives `sm_86`, `9.0` gives `sm_90`, `8.0` gives `sm_80`), passes that one target as `SM_VERSIONS` and in `-arch`, records it in the setup record, and checks with `cuobjdump --list-elf` (from the CUDA toolkit) that `megadock-gpu` contains code for that target; a missing target stops setup. Historical build commands for an `sm_90` box (blind-02 m5 run2 `setup.sh:52-80`, as carried by earlier briefs of this route; replace `sm_90` by the box's target):

```bash
if [[ ! -d baseline-published/cuda-samples/.git ]]; then
    git clone --depth 1 --branch v12.8 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples baseline-published/cuda-samples
fi
git -C baseline-published/cuda-samples describe --tags --exact-match
samples=$(pwd)/baseline-published/cuda-samples
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=0 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ FFTW_INSTALL_PATH=/usr \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include FFTW_LDFLAGS='-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f'
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=1 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ SM_VERSIONS=sm_90 \
    "NVCC=$CUDA_NVCC -Xcompiler -fopenmp -arch=sm_90 -use_fast_math" \
    "INCLUDES=-Isrc -I$CUDA_INCLUDE -I$samples/Common" \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include \
    "LIB=-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f -L$CUDA_LIB -Wl,-rpath,$CUDA_LIB -lcudart -lcufft"
```

  CUDA paths are discovered on the box. In this published release `megadock -h` and `megadock-gpu -h` print their usage and exit with status 255; accept that status only together with the usage text.
- Fixture inputs: `setup.sh` fetches each input's receptor and ligand source from the URL in its `spec`, checks the byte count and SHA-256 recorded there (any mismatch stops the run), and writes the prepared files to the `spec`'s `prepared` paths under the shared run directory by changing only the chain field (column 22) to `R` in the receptor and `L` in the ligand on ATOM, HETATM, ANISOU and TER records, keeping every other byte and line. It records the SHA-256 of every prepared file in its setup record. The URLs, byte counts, SHA-256 values and prepared paths are written in `setup.sh` itself.
- Native complexes: only `fetch_private.sh` fetches them, from the URLs in the inputs' `spec.reference`, and checks their byte counts and SHA-256. `setup.sh`, the adapters and the arms never fetch, copy or read them.
- Evaluator: install PINDER from the pinned source archive (URL and SHA-256 in the materials above and in the view), as run9's excerpt above shows, under the shared run directory or with apt, never under the home directory. After installing it, `setup.sh` checks that the evaluator's interpreter imports `BiotiteDockQ` from `pinder.eval.dockq` (an import only; no private data, no scoring) and stops setup if it does not. `evaluate.sh` reads `model_<rank>.pdb` from `CMP_ARM_OUT` in rank order, scores each against the input's native complex under `CMP_PRIVATE` with BiotiteDockQ and the model's chains `R` and `L` mapped to the native's receptor and ligand chains, and writes `CMP_EVAL_OUT/dockq.json` as one JSON array of the DockQ values in rank order with no other number. Per-model components, if written, go to a separate file.
- Evaluator invocation (correction): BiotiteDockQ is constructed with `parallel_io=False`, so it reads the models in its own process. PINDER's parallel reader starts worker processes with the `spawn` method, which re-imports the main program from its file; a program given to Python on standard input has no such file, and the workers then fail and the pool never returns. `evaluate.sh` carries the evaluator's Python program in its own text (for example in a quoted here-document written with `cat`), writes it at each call to a regular file under `CMP_EVAL_OUT` (for example under `CMP_EVAL_OUT/tmp/`), and runs it as `"$VPY" <that file>`. It never runs `python -` with a here-document or any other standard-input program, and never runs a Python file kept under `harness/`, which is not on the box.
- `cmp_files.json`: `transforms` and `scores` at `out/docking.out`; `coords` at `{"glob": "out/model_*.pdb"}`; `dockq` at `eval/dockq.json`.
- `versions.sh`: for A0 and A2 the `megadock` executable, for A1 and A3 the `megadock-gpu` executable, and for the evaluator the Python interpreter that runs it, each with its version string (the MEGADOCK commit for the MEGADOCK arms, the installed PINDER version for the evaluator).
- Reproduce for A0: no published anchors exist for these inputs. `run_anchors.sh` writes `out/anchors_measured.json` as `{}`, as earlier runs of this route did. `run_command.sh` may run A0's two commands once on input `f1a19` as a smoke check of the build; it compares nothing.

Can MEGADOCK’s GPU implementation make denser docking search affordable, and does that improve pose recovery within a fixed budget?

Use the four unbound PINDER cases examined by blind01’s unit probe. Pin their exact identities, prepared inputs and reference structures before execution. Treat this as a small pilot.

Compare three configurations:

1. CPU execution with standard rotational sampling.
2. GPU execution with the same sampling and scientific settings.
3. GPU execution with the documented denser rotational sampling.

Use MEGADOCK’s existing implementations. Keep scoring settings and the number of retained predictions fixed at 50.

First establish correct execution and scientific agreement between CPU and GPU configurations at identical search settings. Define justified numerical tolerances before examining comparative results.

Then measure whether denser search improves recovery. Report DockQ for the top-ranked prediction and the best of 50 separately. Use reference structures only for evaluation.

Use a small runtime calibration to define feasible budgets. Seal configurations, timing repetitions, comparison rules and the total spending cap before evaluation. Report complete workflow time, GPU activity and billed allocation cost.

Keep three conclusions separate: execution acceleration, scientific agreement at identical settings, and quality changes from additional search. Preserve negative results and budget overruns.

Identify any pipeline contract that cannot express these comparisons. Report that limitation explicitly without substituting a different scientific question.

Limit conclusions to these four cases. Do not infer biological efficacy from docking accuracy.

## Comparison request (science step s29)

This request asks for one comparison-mode run: the arms, fixture inputs, outputs and evaluator exactly as the comparison view (`comparison_view.json`) describes them. It is a recording run on fixture inputs, repeating an earlier recording run of this route with corrections to how the programs are built, how the evaluator is invoked, and how the harness scripts get their data on the box. It is not the seed's main experiment, and the seed's four cases above are not run, fetched or evaluated in it. Preserve the seed above.

What the run does

- Four arms, as the view describes them. A0 is the published baseline (the seed's configuration 1). A1 is the seed's configuration 2. A2 repeats A0's commands and A3 repeats A1's commands, each as separate invocations. The pipeline runs every arm's commands itself; the adapters only check that the input's prepared files exist.
- Four fixture inputs, as the view describes them: holo test-set monomer pairs of four PINDER `2024-02` systems that are not among the seed's four cases. Each input's `spec` names its receptor and ligand sources (URL, byte count, SHA-256), the prepared paths the arms read, and its native complex, which only the evaluator may read.
- The evaluator: PINDER's DockQ implementation at the pinned commit, as the view describes it, scoring each arm's assembled models of one input against that input's native complex.
- Outputs, as the view describes them: the ranked rows of each arm's `docking.out` (transform fields and score field), the coordinates of the assembled models, and the evaluator's DockQ value for each model. They are recorded and compared across arms by the pipeline. No agent computes or reports a comparison.

Which harness files reach the box (correction)

- The pipeline uploads only these files from `harness/` to the box: `setup.sh`, `run_anchors.sh`, `run_command.sh`; `run_evaluation.sh`, `run_units.sh` and `units.json` when they exist; and the sealed comparison files `arms/<arm id>.sh`, `cmp_files.json`, `cmp_extract.json`, `versions.sh`, `fetch_private.sh` and `evaluate.sh`. Any other file written under `harness/` (a Python helper, a JSON list of inputs, a table of published values) never reaches the box. A repair may change only `setup.sh` (or `run_anchors.sh` and `run_command.sh`); the sealed comparison files are never repaired, so a defect in one of them stops the run.
- Every one of these scripts is therefore self-contained: it reads no file under `harness/` except itself, and carries in its own text every list, value and program it needs, or reads it from the variables the pipeline sets (`CMP_INPUT`, `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`, `CMP_OUT`, `CMP_ARM_OUT`, `CMP_EVAL_OUT`, `CMP_PRIVATE`). Write no other file under `harness/`.
- `fetch_private.sh` runs as a separate user with the private directory as its working directory and has no `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`; its output is not kept. It carries in its own text, for each of the four inputs, the native complex's name, URL, byte count and SHA-256 exactly as `spec.reference` gives them in the view, downloads each one, checks its byte count and SHA-256 (a mismatch exits nonzero), and writes it under its working directory at that name.
- `evaluate.sh` takes the input id from `CMP_INPUT` and the native complex's name, byte count and SHA-256 from `spec.reference` in `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`; it reads no input list from any file.

Materials, pins and preparation

- MEGADOCK: the published repository https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK at commit `9575280c875732553266e26adc607dd892b02616`, built twice from the same checkout under `baseline-published/megadock/` in the shared run directory, so that `baseline-published/megadock/megadock`, `baseline-published/megadock/megadock-gpu` and `baseline-published/megadock/decoygen` exist there. The CUDA samples headers come from https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples at tag `v12.8`; they are build dependencies only. The CPU build uses single-precision FFTW exactly as below. The GPU build keeps `-Xcompiler -fopenmp` and `-use_fast_math` and the libraries below, and targets the compute capability of the GPU on this box: `setup.sh` reads it with `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_cap --format=csv,noheader` (for example `8.6` gives `sm_86`, `9.0` gives `sm_90`, `8.0` gives `sm_80`), passes that one target as `SM_VERSIONS` and in `-arch`, records it in the setup record, and checks with `cuobjdump --list-elf` (from the CUDA toolkit) that `megadock-gpu` contains code for that target; a missing target stops setup. Historical build commands for an `sm_90` box (blind-02 m5 run2 `setup.sh:52-80`, as carried by earlier briefs of this route; replace `sm_90` by the box's target):

```bash
if [[ ! -d baseline-published/cuda-samples/.git ]]; then
    git clone --depth 1 --branch v12.8 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples baseline-published/cuda-samples
fi
git -C baseline-published/cuda-samples describe --tags --exact-match
samples=$(pwd)/baseline-published/cuda-samples
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=0 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ FFTW_INSTALL_PATH=/usr \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include FFTW_LDFLAGS='-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f'
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=1 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ SM_VERSIONS=sm_90 \
    "NVCC=$CUDA_NVCC -Xcompiler -fopenmp -arch=sm_90 -use_fast_math" \
    "INCLUDES=-Isrc -I$CUDA_INCLUDE -I$samples/Common" \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include \
    "LIB=-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f -L$CUDA_LIB -Wl,-rpath,$CUDA_LIB -lcudart -lcufft"
```

  CUDA paths are discovered on the box. In this published release `megadock -h` and `megadock-gpu -h` print their usage and exit with status 255; accept that status only together with the usage text.
- Fixture inputs: `setup.sh` fetches each input's receptor and ligand source from the URL in its `spec`, checks the byte count and SHA-256 recorded there (any mismatch stops the run), and writes the prepared files to the `spec`'s `prepared` paths under the shared run directory by changing only the chain field (column 22) to `R` in the receptor and `L` in the ligand on ATOM, HETATM, ANISOU and TER records, keeping every other byte and line. It records the SHA-256 of every prepared file in its setup record. The URLs, byte counts, SHA-256 values and prepared paths are written in `setup.sh` itself.
- Native complexes: only `fetch_private.sh` fetches them, from the URLs in the inputs' `spec.reference`, and checks their byte counts and SHA-256. `setup.sh`, the adapters and the arms never fetch, copy or read them.
- Evaluator: install PINDER from the pinned source archive (URL and SHA-256 in the materials above and in the view), as run9's excerpt above shows, under the shared run directory or with apt, never under the home directory. After installing it, `setup.sh` checks that the evaluator's interpreter imports `BiotiteDockQ` from `pinder.eval.dockq` (an import only; no private data, no scoring) and stops setup if it does not. `evaluate.sh` reads `model_<rank>.pdb` from `CMP_ARM_OUT` in rank order, scores each against the input's native complex under `CMP_PRIVATE` with BiotiteDockQ and the model's chains `R` and `L` mapped to the native's receptor and ligand chains, and writes `CMP_EVAL_OUT/dockq.json` as one JSON array of the DockQ values in rank order with no other number. Per-model components, if written, go to a separate file.
- Evaluator invocation (correction): BiotiteDockQ is constructed with `parallel_io=False`, so it reads the models in its own process. PINDER's parallel reader starts worker processes with the `spawn` method, which re-imports the main program from its file; a program given to Python on standard input has no such file, and the workers then fail and the pool never returns. `evaluate.sh` carries the evaluator's Python program in its own text (for example in a quoted here-document written with `cat`), writes it at each call to a regular file under `CMP_EVAL_OUT` (for example under `CMP_EVAL_OUT/tmp/`), and runs it as `"$VPY" <that file>`. It never runs `python -` with a here-document or any other standard-input program, and never runs a Python file kept under `harness/`, which is not on the box.
- `cmp_files.json`: `transforms` and `scores` at `out/docking.out`; `coords` at `{"glob": "out/model_*.pdb"}`; `dockq` at `eval/dockq.json`.
- `versions.sh`: for A0 and A2 the `megadock` executable, for A1 and A3 the `megadock-gpu` executable, and for the evaluator the Python interpreter that runs it, each with its version string (the MEGADOCK commit for the MEGADOCK arms, the installed PINDER version for the evaluator).
- Reproduce for A0: no published anchors exist for these inputs. `run_anchors.sh` writes `out/anchors_measured.json` as `{}`, as earlier runs of this route did. `run_command.sh` may run A0's two commands once on input `f1a19` as a smoke check of the build; it compares nothing.

- No agent, adapter or harness script computes, prints or asserts any difference between arms, any tolerance or any summary of DockQ values. The pipeline records and compares the outputs.
- Preserve every invocation's files, failures and timeouts as they are. Do not rerun any invocation outside the pipeline's schedule.
- If intake or the harness cannot express this run within these boundaries, report the exact contract gap and stop before paid work.
